overview: The atlas gives “Greenland” one whole-island feature from 1900 to 1914, but that tidy color hides a complicated colonial geography. Most Kalaallit lived in small coastal communities under Danish trade and mission institutions, with major regional differences in language, housing, hunting, travel, and contact. The Royal Greenland Trade monopoly depended on seal hunters while restricting outside commerce. Tasiilaq had gained a trade and mission station in 1894, yet Inughuit territory around later Thule remained outside the old colonial districts; a mission arrived in 1909 and Knud Rasmussen's station in 1910 was private. Danish reach was therefore uneven, especially across remote coasts and the uninhabited ice sheet. This was also an era of Kalaallit initiative. Catechists taught children and kept Greenlandic diaries, writers used print to debate the future, and local knowledge sustained qajaqs, umiaqs, sled teams, clothing, and food work. A 1905 church and school law and 1911 councils changed institutions without ending Copenhagen's authority. Henrik Lund wrote “Nunarput utoqqarsuanngoravit” in 1912; Mathias Storch's Sinnattugaq followed in 1914. The atlas endpoint marks a repaint to Denmark, not a conquest, collapse, or disappearance of families.

periods.title: 1900 to 1904: colonies, communities, and unequal exchange
periods.summary: At the opening of the map interval, Danish monopoly institutions concentrated along inhabited coasts and depended on Kalaallit hunters for export products. The Moravian mission withdrew in 1900, while local households, catechists, traders, and churches continued in different regional settings. Nothing created a new island-wide Greenland state in 1900.

periods.title: 1904 to 1905: church and school enter one legal framework
periods.summary: The Church and School Act took effect on 1 April 1905. It turned West Greenland from a mission field into a deanery and organized children's schooling more systematically. The change remained a Danish colonial law and did not make education identical in every settlement, especially outside the older West Greenland districts.

periods.title: 1905 to 1907: experiments in training, farming, and transport rules
periods.summary: A larger seminary building rose in Nuuk, Jens Chemnitz brought a small Faroese sheep flock south in 1906, and 1907 dog rules formalized regional zones. These changes mattered in particular places. They did not replace marine hunting everywhere or make one national economy from Qaanaaq to Cape Farewell.

periods.title: 1907 to 1909: Greenlandic voices press for change
periods.summary: Greenlandic catechists, teachers, clergy, artists, and writers were already using literacy and colonial institutions to argue about society's future. Their position could be ambivalent: administration needed their language and local authority, while paternalist policy limited equality. This slice marks an intellectual movement, not a sudden awakening on one date.

periods.title: 1909 to 1910: new institutions reach Inughuit country
periods.summary: Gustav Olsen began mission work in the Thule region in 1909, assisted by Sechmann Rosbach and by Olsen's wife Ane Sophie. Knud Rasmussen and Peter Freuchen established a private trading station in 1910. These northern projects expose why the atlas's single color exaggerates uniform Danish administration.

periods.title: 1910 to 1911: a private station and public councils
periods.summary: Thule station exchanged imported materials for fox and polar-bear skins and narwhal tusks, attracting some Inughuit families while seasonal movement continued. Farther south, the 1908 governance law finally took effect in 1911, replacing older boards with municipal councils and two provincial councils for the colonial districts.

periods.title: 1911 to 1912: representation with firm limits
periods.summary: North and South Greenland's provincial councils first met in 1911. Greenlandic representatives could discuss regional matters and propose action, but the councils lacked final decision-making power. In 1912 Copenhagen revised the arrangement and concentrated overall direction in one director, demonstrating that participation and colonial control existed at the same time.

periods.title: 1912 to 1914: writing imagines a Greenlandic future
periods.summary: Henrik Lund completed the Greenlandic poem “Nunarput utoqqarsuanngoravit” in 1912. In 1914 Mathias Storch published Sinnattugaq, the first Greenlandic novel, using a future vision to debate education, authority, and equality. The atlas ends its id that year, although these cultural and political conversations continued.

sections.title: What the map draws, and what it cannot prove

items.text: The index contains one exact Greenland record, marked circa from 1900 to 1914, and it was missing a card. It is distinct from greenland-1960, the modern record already used by the site. Sharing their card would blur colonial rule, later constitutional change, and present self-government.

Only world-1900 contains the exact id. Its decoded geometry is a multipolygon with three components, three rings, and 722 positions, bounded approximately by 72.55 degrees west, 12.56 degrees west, 59.76 degrees north, and 83.58 degrees north. Precision in a file is not precision in colonial control.

Town-center coordinates for Nuuk, Qaqortoq, Ilulissat, Upernavik, Qaanaaq, and Tasiilaq fall just outside the generalized coastline, while nearby landward probes fall inside. That is a cartographic edge effect, not evidence that the settlements vanished. Coastal geometry and historical jurisdiction must be audited separately.

Across all fifty snapshots, this exact feature appears once. The same nine landward probes switch from Denmark in 1880 to Greenland in 1900, back to Denmark in 1914, and to greenland-1960 later. The sequence is database labeling, not four island-wide revolutions.

No other feature shares a topology arc with this ocean-bounded target. The three components represent one large land shape plus two islands in the source geometry. Arc isolation says nothing about who lived where, whose waters were used, or how far officials could travel in practice.

sections.title: Colonial power followed trade routes, not a solid color

items.text: Royal Greenland Trade combined commerce and administration for much of the colonial era and enforced a monopoly that blocked ordinary trade with visiting Europeans. Officials wanted sealing to remain productive. Kalaallit hunters supplied the blubber and skins, while imported guns and goods deepened a relationship of unequal mutual dependence.

Colonial policy encouraged young men to become qajaq hunters because export trade depended on their catch. Fathers, rather than Danish officials, transmitted the essential practical skill. The administration tried to preserve a hunting culture for economic reasons even while describing that same society through paternalist ideas.

The colonial order created ethnic and class divisions. Danish officials occupied senior positions; Kalaallit were steered toward seal hunting; many people of mixed descent worked in trade or mission roles between them. Those categories shaped opportunity, but individuals and households never fit a perfectly stacked social diagram.

The 1908 act separated trade from public administration and created two leaders, but the arrangement proved awkward. A 1912 revision placed overall direction under a single director in Copenhagen. Administrative reorganization changed offices and reporting lines without transferring final sovereignty to the new councils in Greenland.

Around 1911 the colonial districts contained roughly thirteen thousand people and were divided into sixty-two municipalities. Such numbers describe the governed network, not every coast colored by the atlas. Vast ice, remote Northeast Greenland, and Inughuit lands did not become densely administered merely because the polygon was enormous.

sections.title: There was never one uniform Greenlandic household

items.text: West Greenland held the long-established chain of colonies, outposts, churches, and trading places, divided administratively into northern and southern regions. Even there, a colony center and a smaller seasonal settlement offered different work, access to imported goods, schooling, and contact with officials.

Tasiilaq began as a Danish trade and mission station in 1894. Most people in its district still lived in smaller places nearer good hunting rather than crowding into the station. East Greenland's pack ice, dialect, recent mission contact, and settlement pattern made its experience unlike Nuuk's.

In the far northwest, Inughuit communities were outside the old Danish colonial districts. The 1910 Thule station was private, and state takeover came only in 1937. Coloring Qaanaaq and Cape York exactly like established West Greenland colonies projects later territorial administration backward.

Ittoqqortoormiit did not exist in this period; the settlement was founded in 1925 by families moved from the Ammassalik district. The atlas nevertheless colors its future location in 1900. That is useful evidence of the polygon's island-scale ambition and poor evidence of local state presence.

Greenlandic speech itself had regional varieties, while Danish served many colonial offices. A shared written standard and newspaper helped people imagine links across distance, yet language practice still varied by place, schooling, occupation, and contact. “Kalaallit” should not be flattened into one accent or one biography.

sections.title: Hunting, making, moving, and a few experimental sheep

items.text: Qajaqs, larger open umiaqs, and dog sledges were specialized technologies matched to water, ice, cargo, hunting, and region. Their construction joined frames, skins, lashings, balance, and learned weather judgment. Calling them “simple” would be like calling a bicycle simple because it has fewer parts than a ship.

Skin work turned seal, caribou, fox, bird, bear, hare, and dog materials into clothing and equipment. Sinew could become thread; membranes and stomachs became useful containers; chosen hides needed different curing. This expertise joined chemistry-by-practice with careful sewing, repair, and knowledge passed between generations.

Sled designs varied with snow, sea ice, terrain, available wood, and local practice. Drivers learned through oral teaching and close attention to dogs. A team was transport, working partnership, and accumulated environmental knowledge, not merely a furry engine with opinions, although the dogs probably supplied those too.

A 1907 rule divided areas for Greenlandic sled dogs and other dogs, reflecting different regional economies and colonial anxieties about livestock. Sled dogs remained central from Sisimiut northward and in East Greenland, while southern conditions and introduced animals encouraged other arrangements.

In 1906 Greenlandic priest Jens Chemnitz returned with a small Faroese sheep flock for South Greenland. Early households kept sheep as a supplement to hunting and fishing, not as an instant national industry. The experiment was real, regional, and tiny enough that every sheep could ruin a group photograph.

sections.title: Homes, families, gatherings, and growing children

items.text: Turf-walled houses could shelter one family or several. A typical interior had one main room, a raised sleeping platform, and a sunken entrance passage; driftwood, old umiaq skins, turf, and stone insulated the roof. By 1900 glass windows and board walls appeared unevenly in Danish-Greenlandic house forms.

Several families sharing one room created company, warmth, work space, and little modern privacy. It does not follow that every Kalaallit household was communal. Region, season, wealth, available materials, station housing, and family circumstance produced different homes, including imported timber buildings around trade and mission sites.

At aasiviit, people traveled to barter, exchange news, settle disputes, renew alliances, and meet possible spouses. Colonial trading posts gradually reduced the widest mobility, but the social memory matters. A summer gathering was marketplace, message board, reunion, and perhaps dating app, all without charging a battery.

Children learned by watching, helping, listening, and practicing within families as well as through church schools. Hunting, skin preparation, navigation, animal care, stories, and weather judgment could not be mastered from a printed page alone. Exact ages and task divisions varied, so no universal childhood timetable survives.

Thule records show families gathering near the station during winter while some moved to other sites in spring, summer, and autumn as hunting opportunities changed. Station trade altered materials and settlement choices, yet families still organized movement around animals, weather, kin, and their own practical decisions.

sections.title: School meant catechists, language, and uneven access

items.text: Kalaallit catechists often served both as teachers and local church workers. Their core lessons included reading, writing, biblical texts, and Bible history, usually in Greenlandic. A child in a small settlement might therefore learn from a locally rooted teacher whose duties stretched well beyond a modern classroom job.

Catechists kept official work diaries in Greenlandic, recording weather, teaching, church events, and exceptional happenings. Surviving volumes from many settlements span roughly 1880 to 1930. They are precious local voices, although an official diary reflects assigned duties and does not capture every family conversation.

The 1905 law brought church and school under one consolidated framework and marked West Greenland's transition from mission field to church district. It organized schooling more systematically, but curriculum, staffing, travel, weather, and the boundaries of colonial districts still shaped what children could actually receive.

Nuuk's larger seminary building opened during this reform era and supported training for catechists and teachers. The institution helped form a Greenlandic educated elite. Access remained narrow, and its graduates occupied a complicated position as colonial employees who could also criticize unequal policy through language and expertise.

Gustav Olsen trained as a catechist in Nuuk and reached Thule as a missionary in 1909. His wife Ane Sophie appears to have helped with teaching and diaries. That partnership reminds us that archival job titles can hide women's educational labor inside households and mission work.

sections.title: Health, healing, and the limits of colonial records

items.text: Greenlandic families possessed practical knowledge of injury, birth, food, cold, and illness, while colonial stations added uneven access to doctors and imported treatments. The reviewed sources do not support one island-wide medical system. Distance and weather could turn care into a transport problem before diagnosis even began.

Church registers recorded baptisms, marriages, deaths, travel, and communion, but early twentieth-century causes of death were often entered by clergy or officials without medical certification. Those records are invaluable and incomplete. A neat disease total can conceal uncertain diagnosis, local terminology, and missing settlements.

Colonial doctors sometimes interpreted illness through racial theories and labels supposedly unique to Inuit bodies. Modern historians warn that such diagnoses reveal medical power and assumptions as well as symptoms. A doctor's vocabulary should never be mistaken for a neutral photograph of Kalaallit health.

Tuberculosis became devastating in the following decades. A 1924 case shows a sick child moved by dog sled because nursing in a crowded turf home was difficult, while hunger and crowding worsened risk. This near-after evidence illuminates vulnerability but must not be converted into exact 1900 statistics.

Formal training for Greenlanders in midwifery and other health-linked trades existed only in limited form under colonial policy. That scarcity does not mean births occurred without skilled help. It means official archives privilege certified posts and give a thinner view of household expertise, mutual care, and women's work.

sections.title: Water, waste, and the historically honest toilet answer

items.text: No reviewed source demonstrates a uniform piped-water or sewer system across Greenland from 1900 to 1914. Settlements were scattered, housing differed, and later infrastructure histories still emphasize strong local variation. Claims about water must be tied to a particular house, station, season, and source.

The National Museum's typical turf-house description names the main room, sleeping platform, entrance passage, roof, and light openings, but no dedicated bathroom. That silence does not prove where every resident relieved themselves. It does rule out casually installing a modern flush toilet in every reconstructed home.

Trading places included dwellings, warehouses, workshops, provision stores, blubber houses, churches, schools, and sometimes hospitals. These buildings handled very different materials and risks. A station plan can reveal where work occurred, yet it cannot stand in for the sanitation arrangements of outlying camps or family houses.

Families necessarily managed drinking water, washing, food scraps, animal remains, urine, and feces, but the reviewed evidence does not justify one Greenland-wide method. Snow, streams, carried water, shore disposal, containers, and privies require local documentation before they become facts for this exact card.

Toilet verdict: no royal porcelain throne can be issued to every turf house, and no joke about universal filth survives source checking either. The honest answer is regional variation plus a documentation gap. That may be less dramatic, but it keeps modern plumbing and colonial prejudice out of the room.

sections.title: Greenlandic writing speaks from inside the period

items.text: Greenlandic writing had a standardized nineteenth-century orthography, printed books, and the newspaper Atuagagdliutit before 1900. Literacy grew through church and school, while oral traditions continued to preserve history, routes, kinship, humor, and knowledge. Writing expanded the archive; it did not replace speaking, performance, or memory.

Contemporaneous sample: “Nunarput utoqqarsuanngoravit.” In modern spelling it needs no transliteration; a close translation is “Our country, now that you have become very old.” Henrik Lund wrote this Greenlandic patriotic poem in 1912. It later became an anthem, but the 1937 melody lies outside this card.

A second exact-window sample is the 1914 book title “SingnagtugaK,” now spelled “Sinnattugaq,” meaning “A Dream.” It is Mathias Storch's first Greenlandic novel, printed in Copenhagen. The title is Greenlandic; its publication place and colonial printing route should remain visible rather than being relocated to Nuuk.

Sinnattugaq imagined Greenland's future in order to discuss education, mistrust, marriage authority, and unequal relations with Danes. Calling it merely the “first novel” misses its achievement: a Kalaallit author used an imported literary form to make colonial society answer an inside voice.

Photographs from 1890 to 1960 preserve clothing, buildings, boats, work, families, and colonial encounters, but cameras also frame and select. Names, captions, photographers, and collection history matter. An anonymous posed image cannot by itself prove what every person wore daily or thought about the photographer.

The 1908 governance act created municipal councils and provincial councils, which began operating in 1911. Municipal members were Greenlanders elected locally; provincial representatives were chosen indirectly. These bodies opened structured political discussion, although Danish officials chaired the provincial level and Copenhagen retained final authority.

Municipal councils dealt with poverty assistance, support, public order, and spending for common needs. Their records can reveal decisions close to daily life. They covered the recognized colonial municipalities, not an empty ice sheet or every community that the atlas places inside one island polygon.

In world-1914 the exact Greenland id disappears and every landward control probe is assigned to denmark-1815. No border feature records a conquest, surrender, evacuation, or new treaty at that seam. The atlas changes which label owns the same island geometry while Danish colonial rule continues.

The modern greenland-1960 id begins much later and already has its own card. It belongs to a different constitutional and political story. Keeping this 1900 record separate prevents modern self-government, citizenship, transport, hospitals, and household infrastructure from leaking backward into colonial daily life.

The safest ending is wonderfully undramatic: the software swaps labels while people keep waking, teaching, hunting, sewing, praying, arguing, writing, fetching water, and worrying about supper. Greenland did not fall off the map; only this exact database id did. That distinction is the card's final achievement.

ending.text: The exact Greenland id ends in 1914 because the atlas repaints the same island as Denmark. No reviewed source records Greenland falling, being conquered, or becoming Danish in that year; it was already under an uneven Danish colonial system. Kalaallit communities continued, and the trade, mission, councils, writing, and regional ways of life continued changing. The later greenland-1960 record is kept separate because it represents another constitutional era. This card therefore leaves fell null and names no single successor: 1914 is an editorial label seam, not the end of a people, place, or society.
